chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from 'Asim from 'Anbasah ibn Mus'abb said:

I saw Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) in Mina walking and riding. I told myself that I would ask him when I enter upon him, but he initiated the narration and said: Indeed, Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) used to leave his house on foot when he threw the Jamarat (stones at the pillars in Hajj). And my house today is further from his than his house was from his [previous location], so I ride until I reach him. When I arrive at him, I walk until I throw the Jamarat.
The way to reconcile these two narrations is to interpret them as indicating a type of recommended status (mustahabb) rather than obligatory (fard) or compulsory (ijbar).

key_terms.أَبَا عَبدِ اللّهِ ع: Abu Abdillah (Imam al-Sadiq), peace be upon him
key_terms.رَمَى الْجِمَارَ: Throwing stones at the pillars during Hajj

ai.seo_question: Is walking during the stoning of the Jamarat obligatory or recommended in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Istibsar illustrates the flexibility in Haj rituals by contrasting the practice of Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn (AS), who walked to the Jamarat, with the narrator’s practice of riding due to distance before walking for the ritual itself. Shaykh al-Tusi uses this to establish that walking is a recommended act (mustahabb) rather than a strict obligation (wajib), highlighting the Shia jurisprudential principle of accommodating physical ease without invalidating the rite. This distinction underscores the balance between ritual precision and practical mercy in Shia fiqh.
